'My last opportunity': Old school approach serving McInnes to the end
As the two-minute bell sounds in the Cronulla sheds on Saturday night, Cameron McInnes will take a moment to pause and reflect.
Depending on how the next 80 minutes play out, he could be about to run on to an NRL field for the final time.
It's the same routine McInnes has followed all season, the Sharks enforcer aware his time in the NRL could end at any moment.
Those emotions have never been more real this week, Cronulla to play North Queensland in a sudden-death final at Allianz Stadium.
McInnes chats Cowboys blockbuster
Win and McInnes' career continues for another week. Lose and one of the game's last old-school forwards will walk off the field for the final time.
"I have a moment before each game where I have a thought to myself, 'this could be my last game'," McInnes said.
"Last year when I did my knee, [before that game] I didn't think it was going to be the end of my season. At some point I'll have played my last game and that is important."

A tough, rugged forward who never gives an inch, McInnes looks like he was plucked straight out of the 1980s and plays like it too.
The NRL record holder for most tackles in a match, the forward has set the standard at every club he's played for.
After making his debut with the Rabbitohs, McInnes joined the Dragons in 2017 before his final season in the Red V was over before it even began when he tore his ACL during the 2021 pre-season.
He then moved to the Sharks in 2022 and was tasked with bringing a hard edge to the Shire. It's no coincidence Cronulla have made the finals in every season he has spent with the club.
*Almost all of Cameron McInnes's record breaking tackles count
"He's such an inspirational leader for our team," co-captain Blayke Brailey said. "He's changed our club and the way we play, the way we prepare for games since he turned up.
"He's done so much for our game and our team and hopefully we can send him off on the high he deserves because he's given every part of his body for the game and our team and deserves northing more than to go out on a high."
Brailey isn't joking when he said McInnes has given every part of his body to the sport.
The 32-year-old has undergone 15 operations throughout his career. Ironically, given how much defensive work he does, McInnes' shoulders are one of the few body parts to get through his career largely unscathed.
Cameron McInnes Try
There were fears his playing days were finished 12 months ago when he suffered a second ACL rupture. The injury brought a premature end to his 2025 campaign but McInnes returned to the field earlier this season and hasn't skipped a beat.
"I've had some small surgeries and a few major ones," McInnes said. "I'm lucky I'm quite routine-based. That's important when you're coming out of surgery because you need to do everything right.
"I don't enjoy being injured but I do enjoy that process. That helps me get back on the field and I've learnt that you'll never feel good out there. Some players have to feel like a Ferrari, that's not me, I don't have to feel like that."
While his playing style was plucked from a past era, McInnes has managed to adapt and thrive in the modern age of fast-paced rugby league.
The trend towards undersized middle forwards has led to a new role for the forward, who moved from hooker to lock when he joined the Sharks.
While many feared players such as McInnes would struggle to find a home in the modern game, the veteran believes he has been a major beneficiary of the changes.

NRL Casualty Ward: Walker goes down with calf injury
The Rabbitohs' have been dealt a body blow at Allianz Stadium on Friday night with spiritual leader Cody Walker suffering a calf injury.
Walker collapsed to the turf with no one around him in the 31st minute and immediately signalled to the bench that he was in trouble.
The 36-year-old felt for his calf and hobbled to the sideline where he was visibly distressed as the reality set in that his season looks over.
Walker sat on the bench for the second half with ice on his calf and carrying a crutch.
The Warriors have received a huge boost ahead of their qualifying final against the Dolphins with gun forward Jackson Ford set to return from a pectoral injury.
After making a dynamic start to the season in which he averaged 161 run metres and 41 tackles per game, Ford suffered the injury in Round 16 against the Cowboys and initial fears were he could miss the rest of the year.
Ford has been named on the bench for the blockbuster Go Media Stadium showdown against the Dolphins, who get Selwyn Cobbo (ankle), back-rower Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (knee) and five-eighth Kodi Nikorima (hamstring) back for their first ever final.
Nikorima and Finefeuiaki were given last week off to get over niggling injuries ahead of the finals.
The Roosters also have a star forward returning for their qualifying final against Penrith with Angus Crichton back after 11 games out with a foot injury.
Also back on deck at the Roosters are Victor Radley (concussion) and a posse of stars who were rested in Round 27 including James Tedesco , Daly Cherry-Evans and Rob Toia .
The Rabbitohs have Tallis Duncan back from a hamstring injury but will be without veteran back-rower Euan Aitken for the rest of the season after he fractured his scapula in the win over the Roosters.
The injury is a cruel blow for 31-year-old Aitken, who was on the verge of playing in just the second finals match of his 223-game career.
Aitken's only finals appearance came with the Dragons in his debut season in 2015.

The Storm also lost halfback Jahrome Hughes to a hamstring injury late in the first half after he was twisted awkwardly while trying to clean up a loose ball.
Hughes will be sent for scans and faces a nervous wait for the results with the Kiwis' World Cup opener just six weeks away.

No strangers to facing off in finals - both the Sharks and Cowboys will be hoping to shake off their most recent form in this elimination final.

Last round, they were outplayed and out-enthused 50-30 by a Raiders side with nothing to lose, so will be looking to aim up for this must-win clash.
The two clubs have plenty of post-season history as well, so will be aiming to reset their campaigns and claim another win against their finals rivals.

History lesson: Last time the contenders met in a final
A whole new competition starts this weekend as eight contenders go into battle across four matches in three days with one goal in mind.
The Panthers have proven themselves the masters of finals football across the past five years while the Roosters (2002, 2013, 2018, 2019), Sharks (2016), Cowboys (2015), Rabbitohs (2014) and Knights (2001) all have premierships to their name in the NRL era.
The Dolphins are in their first ever finals series and their opponents the Warriors have been here 10 times but never come away with a title.
With two sudden-death showdowns and two qualifying finals coming up this weekend, NRL.com takes a look at the most recent September clash between the sides.
Knights v Rabbitohs
2020 elimination final
The Rabbitohs and Knights have only met once in finals football, and it came in exactly the same circumstances as Friday night at Allianz Stadium.
Six years ago, South Sydney and Newcastle finished sixth and seventh respectively before meeting in a sudden-death elimination final.
Now, with the Rabbitohs sixth and the Knights seventh again, history is repeating itself as the two sides prepare to do battle for a place in the semi-finals.
There is still plenty of familiar faces from that 2020 clash.
Match Highlights: Rabbitohs v Knights
Alex Johnston, Campbell Graham, Cody Walker, Tevita Tatola and Cameron Murray were all part of the Rabbitohs side that night six years ago, while Dane Gagai, who will now wear a Knights jersey, also featured for South Sydney.
Newcastle has just three players remaining from that team in Kalyn Ponga, Bradman Best and Jacob Saifiti.
And if Friday night follows the script from 2020, South Sydney will be hoping for a repeat of the result.
The Rabbitohs blew the Knights away 46-20, with Johnston crossing twice alongside Tatola, two names who will again feature in the elimination final six years later.
Alex Johnston finds the line during the Bunnies' 46-20 win over the Knights in the 2020 elimination final.
Roosters v Panthers
2024 qualifying final
The Roosters and Panthers know each other all too well when it comes to September football.
Their last three finals meetings have all come in the qualifying final, and once again, they find themselves in exactly the same position.
Their most recent showdown came in 2024, when Penrith began its march towards a fourth straight premiership with a commanding 30-10 victory over the Roosters at BlueBet Stadium.
Panthers v Roosters – Finals Week 1, 2024
There is still plenty of familiar faces from that clash, with the Panthers’ champion core and the Roosters’ star-studded spine preparing to renew one of the competition’s fiercest finals rivalries.
Penrith has won four of its past five finals meetings with the Roosters, but with a preliminary-final spot and a precious week off on the line, history will count for little when these two heavyweight clubs collide again.
Yep, he's back!

2024 semi-final
The Sharks and Cowboys have plenty of finals history, and their most recent meeting could provide the perfect blueprint for another high-stakes showdown.
The two clubs have met six times in finals football, with the teams splitting those matches at three apiece but it was the Sharks who had the last laugh.
Sharks v Cowboys – Finals Week 2, 2024
When the sides met in the 2024 semi-final at Allianz Stadium, Cronulla held on for a 26-18 victory to book a place in the preliminary final and end the Cowboys’ campaign.
Braydon Trindall played a starring role that night, scoring twice, and now, two years on, he’ll return from injury with another chance to make his mark.
This time, there is no second chance.
With both sides fighting to keep their premiership dreams alive, Saturday afternoon’s clash promises another chapter in a finals rivalry that has produced plenty of drama over the years.

'No one gave us a chance': Chasing pack desperate to defy history
Cronulla captain Blayke Brailey will draw on NSW's unexpected State of Origin series victory as the Sharks look to defy history by becoming the first team in more than three decades to win the NRL premiership from outside the top four.
It's been 31 years since Terry Lamb led the Bulldogs from sixth place to premiership glory in 1995. While plenty of clubs have come close, the challenge of winning four-straight sudden death finals has proved an insurmountable task.
It's a stat this year's contenders are determined to change, with the Sharks leading a group of teams desperate to rewrite the record books.
Brailey made his NSW debut during this year's series and returned from a broken arm to help the Blues defy history when they upset the Maroons in a Suncorp Stadium decider.
Few gave Laurie Daley's men a chance when they travelled north for Game Three and Brailey said Cronulla will adopt a similar mindset throughout the finals campaign.
"We have the underdog mentality and we all enjoy that approach," Brailey told NRL.com. "No one gives us a chance but it's similar to the Origin series in Game Three when no one gave us a chance. We found it a way and we turned it around.
"People thought we'd just turn up and lose and I'm sure in this finals series people just expect the same. We know what it takes now to deal with that pressure. We've got a few players in our side that love the underdog mentality so we're taking it all in and excited for the weeks to come."
Trindall raring to return for Cowboys clash
Cronulla have received a major boost for Saturday's clash with North Queensland at Allianz Stadium with five-eighth Braydon Trindall named to return from a dislocated shoulder.
The Sharks are in a familiar position entering this year's finals series, Craig Fitzgibbon's men also finishing fifth last season before surging to the preliminary final.
The Cowboys don't have to look too far for inspiration in their bid for the premiership, with Jason Taumalolo and Coen Hess playing a key role in the club's charge from eighth to the 2017 grand final.
North Queensland have also received a major boost in recent weeks with star halfback Tom Dearden making a successful return from an ankle injury.
Also looking to defy history this year are the Rabbitohs and Knights, who will do battle in a Friday night blockbuster at Allianz Stadium to kick off the weekend.
Tom Dearden Try
Both teams also have a track record of deep finals runs from outside the top four, with Newcastle progressing to the preliminary final in 2013 after finishing seventh on the ladder.
Fullback Kalyn Ponga has returned to the form that saw him claim the Dally M Medal in 2023 and has the potential to emulate Reece Walsh's stunning run to the premiership with the Broncos last year.
South Sydney went from seventh to a prelim the last time they played finals football in 2022.
The Rabbitohs are peaking at the right time of year, with star centre Latrell Mitchell back on deck and powerful back-rower David Fifita back to his damaging best.
Latrell Mitchell returns for the Rabbitohs
With finals experience spread across the park, South Sydney captain Cameron Murray is confident his team has the talent to upstage their more fancied rivals.
"We're not paying too much attention to the history books," Murray said. "We're paying attention to the footy we can play and the product we can put on the field.
"If we're disciplined and we turn up with the right attitude, I'm confident we can be successful in the finals.
"We have a lot of big game experience in the team so that helps, but for us it's about our discipline and turning up to play the footy we know we can play."

The family heartbreak driving young Shark's finals bid
Cronulla young gun Riley Jones has opened up on his emotional journey to the NRL as he looks to honour his late father's legacy in Saturday's sudden-death final.
The centre will play just his second match for the Sharks when they take on North Queensland in an elimination final at Allianz Stadium.
Jones' dad Shane lost his battle with leukaemia in 2021, with the youngster using that pain as motivation on a rugby league journey that saw him play a solitary game for the Knights in 2023 while living with Kalyn Ponga before a fresh opportunity emerged with the Sharks last year.
Riley Jones Try
Having ended a 1099-day wait to make his second NRL appearance last weekend, the 24-year-old knows his father will be looking down with a smile when he runs on to Allianz Stadium on Saturday night.
"I feel safe out there and confident knowing that he's watching," Jones told NRL.com. "I wish he could be here but I know he's watching.
"My family's been amazing since he died. Mum has been great and I've got an amazing partner so that helps make a situation like this a lot easier.
"My brother wants to do something to help raise awareness for leukaemia so he's shaved his head which is pretty special to see. He presented my Sharks jersey last week. He's pretty shy so for him to step out of his comfort zone and do that was special."

"I learnt a lot off him growing up. He coached me all the way through juniors, there's a couple of other boys who played under him so it's cool to see those boys' journeys come to life and know dad had a little bit of an impact on their journey."

items.title: How do you get from eighth to a grand final? ‘A prime Jason Taumalolo helps’ - SMH.com.au
items.snippet: How do you get from eighth to a grand final? ‘A prime Jason Taumalolo helps’    SMH.com.au
items.body_excerpt:
Coen Hess doesn’t need to ponder long when asked what it takes for a team to rise from eighth to thrust themselves into an NRL grand final.
“A prime Jason Taumalolo and Michael Morgan helps,” the Cowboys enforcer says with a laugh, recalling North Queensland’s scintillating 2017 finals campaign.
That season marked Hess as an NRL player – bursting onto the scene to garner a State of Origin call-up for Queensland as an impact back rower. Even playing most of his footy off the bench, the now 30-year-old scored 13 tries and ran for a career-best 108 metres a game.
Jason Taumalolo carried the Cowboys on his back in 2017. Can he do it again? Getty Images
He and Taumalolo are the last men standing from that 2017 charge, in which the Cowboys fell to the Melbourne Storm at the final hurdle.
No side has replicated the feat since, with every decider determined between two teams who completed the regular season inside the top four.
It was a fortuitous run, Hess recalls, as North Queensland needed the Dragons to lose their round 26 clash with the Bulldogs after the Cowboys fell to the Broncos earlier in the week in a run of five defeats in their past six games.
But when St George-Illawarra succumbed, a window opened. Coincidentally, Hess and his teammates faced the same rivals – the Sharks – as they will on Saturday night from the same position. It’s the seventh time they will square off in a finals’ campaign.
History of Cowboys v Sharks in NRL finals
2013 elimination final: Cronulla 20 def North Queensland 18 in a clash marred by controversy after Beau Ryan crossed in the corner in what was the seventh tackle of the set, after a miscount had ensued.
2015 semi-final: North Queensland 39 def Cronulla as Johnathan Thurston set up two tries and another three linebreaks to book a preliminary final berth en route to a maiden title.
2016 preliminary final: Cronulla 32 def North Queensland 20, with the Cowboys’ three tries in the final 10 minutes not enough to overcome a sluggish start. The week before, North Queensland had fought a 90-minute thriller against the Broncos in Townsville.
2017 elimination final: North Queensland 15 def Cronulla 14, with Michael Morgan kicking an extra time field goal after the Cowboys trailed 8-2 at halftime.
2022 qualifying final: North Queensland 32 def Cronulla 30 in a contest Coen Hess describes as “one of the best wins I’ve been a part of” after Valentine Holmes slotted a two-point field goal after 92 minutes.
2024 semi-final: Cronulla 26 def North Queensland 18, as a Braydon Trindall masterclass – scoring twice and setting up another try – guided the Sharks home.
The season has not been smooth for the Cowboys – their historic 82-10 capitulation against the Roosters, and a heavy 50-30 loss to Canberra each occurring at home in their last five. No side in 2026’s top 12 have conceded as many as North Queensland’s 652 points.
But momentum, Hess believes, can be wrestled back quickly, as 2017 proved.
“One win can really springboard you and give you a lot of confidence, and I think we just rode the high for as long as we could. We were just grateful to be in the position we were – we didn’t even know we were making finals, so we just got thrust into the finals and went on a run,” Hess says.
“This year, the way the games go, anyone can beat anyone on their given day, so it’s just a matter of turning up each week, playing like it’s going to be your last game.
“We haven’t really spoken about it [the 2017 campaign]. During the year you make running comments here and there, but it’s not something we’ve leant on.”
In their three finals victories en route to the grand final, Morgan and Taumalolo struck up a dominant combination.
On the back of Taumalolo’s 756 running metres and 13 tackle busts across those outings, Morgan scored and set up a try in each encounter to overcome the Sharks (15-14), Eels (24-16) and Roosters (29-16).
Coen Hess believes one win is all it can take for the Cowboys to spark a surprising finals run.

NRL Match Preview: Week 1 Finals v Cowboys
Cronulla have lost the recently re-signed Hohepa Puru to an illness 24 hours out from their elimination final.
No other changes ahead of the 5th-placed Sharks hosting the 8th-placed Cowboys at Allianz Stadium tomorrow night at 7:50pm.
Cronulla has hosted Week 1 Finals games at Ocean Protect Stadium in recent years, but a decision was made to move it to the bigger ground in Moore Park.
No complaints from Sharks coach Craig Fitzgibbon though, "We're super excited about playing at Allianz Stadium. It's one of the best stadiums in the country, and it's got that big game atmosphere about it, and that's where we want to be."
"We've worked all year to get to this point, and we want to play in big games so we're super excited about that."
They're super excited to welcome Braydon Trindall back from a shoulder injury as well.
The Sharks half broke the club record for most try-assists in a season with 30 earlier in the year.
His halves partner Nicho also has 23, which means they have the most try assists (53) by a halves combination in recent memory.
"In my opinion it's been his (Trindall's) strongest season for the Sharks and he's grown up a lot and understands his position within the team and how commanding he can be," the Sharks coach said.
"I think also his combination with Nicho is probably the strongest it's been this season, so looking forward to getting him back."
Coming up against a North Queensland side that Cronulla have met six times in finals since 2013.
Both sides have won three apiece out of those encounters with the Cowboys knocking out the Sharks on their way to the 2015 title.
Then the black, white and blue did the same on their route to winning the club's first premiership in 2016.
The Sharks have won three out of the four finals matches played between them at Allianz Stadium.
"It's semi-finals, so the most important thing is who gets it done tomorrow night," Fitzgibbon expressed.
"They've got some wonderfully talented players and have had some really strong performances this year, so we know what they can bring, but we know what we can bring too, and it's whoever brings it on the day."
Fitzgibbon is now the first Cronulla coach in the club's history to make five straight finals appearances.
His Sharks have won three of their past five Finals games, with preliminary final losses to Penrith in 2024 and Melbourne in 2025.
Cronulla has won 14 of the past 17 games against North Queensland, but the Cowboys won their last encounter in Round 8 in Townsville 46-34.
The Sharks have lost their past two games, and four of five going into this week, but have not lost three straight since 2024.
Cronulla receives the fewest penalties, concedes the equal third most in the NRL, and they also receive the equal most ruck infringements.
Nicho Hynes needs one point to become the outright third all-time Sharks points scorer, currently level with Luke Covell on 948 points.
Hynes is also chasing his 100th NRL win in what will be his 148th NRL game with a 67%-win record.
Sione Katoa requires one try to bring up his 100th NRL try, with only Andrew Ettingshausen (165), Ronaldo Mulitalo (112) and David Peachey (110) having done so for Cronulla.

‘Anger, surprise, and then joy’: Todd Payten rides emotional rollercoaster at judiciary, says 50-point stat ready to fall
If the Cowboys are to break a 118-year-old curse, then they’ll have one man to thank for keeping their season alive.
There are any number of Cowboys stars who can help coach Todd Payten keep their season going this weekend, but it’s the club’s secret weapon off the field who may have played the biggest role leading into Saturday’s elimination final.
Tom Hancock played a dozen games in the National Youth Competition for North Queensland and then spent eight seasons playing reserve grade, but his most valuable contribution came on Tuesday night at the judiciary .
Former player Tom Hancock helped Reuben Cotter avoid a ban at the judiciary. Picture: Brendan Radke.
Cowboys co-captain Reuben Cotter was facing a two-game ban for a high shot on Raiders legend Josh Papalii, and things didn’t look great when the panel found him guilty.
But Hancock – who represented him on Tuesday – had one more trick to play and got his client a downgrade, which means Cotter is free to face the Sharks, with Hancock helping him twice at the judiciary in the space of four weeks.
“I think he’s had four cases for us this year and a 100 per cent strike rate, so he’s super smart,” Payten said.
“The way he conducted things on Tuesday night was a masterclass and I think he was well prepared, very good at his craft, and I’m glad he’s representing our clients.”
Others you may like
Payten, Cotter and Hancock appeared via video link on Tuesday and rode a wave of emotions as the different verdicts came through.
Cotter would have missed two games if he had been found guilty. Picture: Ian Hitchcock/Getty Images
“Anger, surprise, and then joy. They’re the three emotions in the space of 15 minutes, but we’re here now and everyone’s super excited and looking forward to tomorrow night,” Payten said, thrilled to have his representative lock available.
“We’ve seen him play Origin and how reliable he is in that arena. Finals is a similar pace, and to have someone with the ability to play 80 minutes in that environment is pretty crucial for us.
“Every team would love to have a player like ‘Reubs’, and I’m glad he’s playing tomorrow.”
The Cowboys boast one of the most dynamic attacks in the league, but they also leaked more points than any of the top eight sides.
They are coming off a 50-30 loss last week and also conceded a staggering 82 against the Roosters, with no team in history winning the comp after giving up 50.
The Cowboys have had some bad defensive performances this year, with history suggesting they can’t win the comp. Picture: Ian Hitchcock/Getty Images
More Coverage
“We get past it. This is a new competition,” Payten said of last week’s loss.
“We’ve had some up-and-down moments throughout the season. I think there are probably two or three teams within the competition that haven’t had those, so we’re not on our own. We know our best footy is good enough and we’re here to play well.
“The game has gotten so quick, it’s changed so much over 18 months. I think two teams have made the final before (after conceding 50) and got beaten in the GF. It’s going to happen eventually, so why not now?”

“I am very excited … it's my first ever finals appearance, so very excited and I can't wait to rip in on Saturday night,” Purdue said.
“It's all pretty new to me, to be honest … we had a training session (today), we trained really well and it sort of didn't feel really much different.
“But talking to some of the leaders and more experienced guys, they're saying through the back-end of the week, that's when the nerves start to kick in and a bit more pressure hits your way.
“(For now) I feel like it's just another week and another game to play.
“Obviously it's a do-or-die match, but that's what's so exciting about it and I can't wait.
Jaxon Purdue with fans at the club's opening training session in the lead up to their finals match against the Sharks. ©North Queensland Cowboys
“It means a lot to us this final series, but I think to the whole of North Queensland, our fan base, it's a massive, massive thing for everyone here.
“It's a great community and everyone gets behind us.
“I still remember as a kid when the Cowboys would make the finals, I used to race home and that'd be the best thing and most exciting day for me – to watch the Cowboys play in the finals.
“I still remember that 2022 match when they won against Sharks at Shark Park and it's a pretty cool experience to be able to finally play in a finals game and to put that Cowboys jersey on for a final … is very exciting."

Like others in his team have conceded, Purdue admits consistency has been the side’s biggest weakness this season as their fought their way to an eighth-place finish.
However, he felt his side deserved to be in the play-offs and knew what they needed to do in order to upset the fifth-placed Cronulla side.
“In our meeting (this morning), we talked about how the past five weeks don't really matter and it's how you show up on a final game and play; and how you prepare for that game,” Purdue told NRL.com.
“Because it is a do-or-die, you have got to scrap the past weeks out of your memory bank and really switch on.
“From now on in, you have got to play your best game every game, otherwise you'll be knocked out.

“Sharks have such a good spine and such a good team where we can't give them many opportunities, because they'll pounce on it.
“We've got our homework to do this week ... and then we will know what we've got to do to beat them Saturday night.”

Trindall ready to spark Sharks in high-stakes comeback
Sharks captain Blayke Brailey is confident Braydon Trindall's return from a shoulder injury will unlock halfback Nicho Hynes as Cronulla look to kickstart their finals campaign.
Trindall is set to be named on Tuesday afternoon in the Sharks squad for Saturday's sudden-death clash with the Cowboys at Allianz Stadium.
The comeback comes just four weeks after the five-eighth dislocated his shoulder in a Round 24 loss to the Raiders, with Cronulla winning just one of three games without Trindall.
Trindall dislocates shoulder while scoring try
Despite missing the last month of the season, Trindall still finished the year as the NRL's try-assist leader, with a club record 30 try assists, and Brailey backed the playmaker to make an instant impact on Saturday night.
"It's a massive in for us," Brailey said. "He's a great player. Everyone can see how good he is for our side. He brings so much calmness and joy to our game, not only with the ball but without it too.
"He's massive for us, he's looking fit and healthy and I'm keen to see him run out there again."

Trindall and Hynes have developed a unique combination over the past few years, the pair's contrasting styles complementing each other nicely on the field.
While Hynes largely orchestrates the team's attack and steers the side around the park, Trindall takes charge in the attacking 20-metre zone to create opportunities for the Sharks outside backs.
Trindall's short kicking game is also among the best in the business and Cronulla have used it to lethal effect this season.
The halves partnership has played a key role in the Sharks' emergence as a perennial finals contender, but the challenge now is to turn a top-eight finish into a premiership.
Tricky in everything
"Their partnership is huge for us," Brailey said. "They kick really well, if one's running, the other will steer the team around. They're both sevens in their own right and they both can produce great plays for our side.
"They calm each other really well. They both drive the team, steer the direction of where we're going and off the field they're so close. Tricky's return will bring out the best in all of us, not just Nicho but the whole side."
Trindall will need to hit the ground running if the Sharks are to keep their season alive with a victory over the Cowboys.
North Queensland prevailed in a high-scoring affair when the two sides faced off in Round 8 and the recent return of halfback Tom Dearden has helped lift the Cowboys to another level.
Kennedy and Trindall win it with two massive plays
While Trindall's attacking impact attracts much of the attention, his teammates feel the playmaker's defence often flies under the radar.
That, according to prop Addin Fonua-Blake, will prove crucial on Saturday night.
"It's no secret how big a part he plays for us," Fonua-Blake said. "Him and Nicho complement each other so well. If we're going to do anything special in this competition, we're going to need them both for this end of the season.
"Those two can do things in a game you can't coach, that's what makes them great. When you're defending your line, you get the ball back and they can kick a 40-20.
"Then seeing the way they fight in defence, it's a good feeling seeing your halves putting their bodies on the line like that."
